interview / @cube_rat / music journal, est. nine years ago

Nine years of cube_rat

An interview with the person behind one of Instagram's most devoted music journals.

scroll to begin
Side A, track 1

How does it feel to have a music reviewing account for so long? What keeps you going?

Nine years of cube_rat. Honestly, I'm a little surprised myself! It started with something very simple, posting about whatever I was listening to. Slowly, those posts grew into reviews and other things I wanted to share, and somehow, here we are.

There have been moments when I've thought about quitting. But whenever that happens, I remind myself that nobody is putting pressure on me to do this. It's something I choose to do, mostly as a music journal for myself. If someone else finds it interesting or discovers something through it, that makes me happy. What keeps me going is the music. There's just no end to the brilliant, strange, interesting and completely hypnotic stuff people keep creating. Music has helped me through some of my darkest moments and been there to celebrate the most amazing ones. Sometimes it helps me understand what I'm feeling; sometimes it gives me a way to escape the world for a while.

This might sound a little weird, but I almost feel like I owe music something. It's this abstract thing, yet it has given me so much over the years. Sharing it feels like a small way of giving something back. And thanks to this account, every Friday feels like Christmas. You never know what's waiting for you or which release is about to hit you with a thousand watts. A million thanks to the musicians who are brave enough to put their work out into the world. Alongside being my own journal, I hope cube_rat gives people a place to discover that music and musicians a small space where their art can be heard.

Every Friday feels like Christmas.
Rewind

How did you start @cube_rat?

Music was around me long before cube_rat. My older siblings listened to a lot of it, and I was always digging through their collections. I think I was about eight when I had my own albums on CD, so this has been part of my life for pretty much as long as I can remember.

Before starting the account, I worked in early childhood education, where listening to music while working wasn't really an option. Later, I moved into office work. After a couple of months, I realised I was playing the same old favourites week after week, and decided to challenge myself to find something new. Whenever I didn't have meetings, the headphones went on. Pretty soon, I wanted to keep track of what I was discovering, and that became cube_rat.

The first posts were only a sentence or two. Over time, I wanted to give a little more to the people following the account and to the musicians whose work I was sharing. That led to longer reviews, collaborations and different kinds of special posts.

The account has gone through plenty of phases, mostly depending on how much time I've had. At the moment, I try to post once or twice a week, and I also curate the "Album of the Month" series for MusicReviewWorld. Everything I post is something I like to some degree. If a release does nothing for me, it doesn't end up on the feed. And when something really connects, I give it the "cube_rat recommendation" mention.

Old favourites, new ones

Do you approach reviewing music differently when you already know and love an artist compared with discovering someone completely new?

Absolutely. When an artist has already made something you love, you bring that connection into whatever comes next. There's excitement, but also a little tension. You want to feel that thing again. Because of that, the reaction can be much stronger in either direction.

Converge is a good example. I knew them before Axe to Fall came out in 2009, but that was the album that really put them into regular rotation for me. Then All We Love We Leave Behind arrived in 2012 and became another massive release in my life. During the long wait for the next album, I also dug into their older cult classics. By the time The Dusk in Us arrived in 2018, I was very excited. But personally, it didn't deliver in the same way as the previous record. I kept following their releases over the years without being quite as impressed, until Hum of Hurt this year somehow blew my mind all over again.

Discovering someone completely new is a different kind of pleasure. There's no history to live up to and no particular sound I'm hoping to hear. I feel more open. You press play, see where it takes you, and either move on or suddenly find yourself listening to something amazing.

What makes it click

How do you distinguish a good song? What separates an interesting release from a track that doesn't feel that unique for you?

I wish I had a clear recipe for this, but I really don't. I've thought about it quite a lot, and one thing I keep coming back to is timing. A song might do absolutely nothing for me one week and hit perfectly the next. What works during a busy workday can be completely different from what I want to hear on a quiet evening at the beach. The biggest thing, though, is the feeling and atmosphere a song creates. That can come from almost anywhere, the soundscape and mixing, a bassline, the drums, the tone of someone's voice, a vocal melody or some unexpected little detail. When those things make me feel something, that's when the song connects.

And it doesn't always need to be particularly surprising. Recently, I came across a simple indie rock track called "Let Down" by The Yaz Band. There's no huge trick or astonishing twist in it. The arrangement just works so well that I keep coming back for another listen. Sometimes that's all it takes.

The people behind the playlists

Your playlists and recommendations can introduce people to music they might never encounter otherwise. What role do you think curators play in the way people discover music today?

A huge one! I have my own favourite Instagram accounts whose recommendations I've learned to trust. That's one of the best things about following someone for years, you gradually get to know their taste and how it connects with yours. There are also accounts doing brilliant work whose recommendations rarely fit what I enjoy. That doesn't make their work any less valuable. It's a bit like friends. You know which friend is likely to recommend your next favourite album, and which one will enthusiastically send you something that leaves you completely cold. For me, that personal connection matters. I still trust the people behind recommendations more than AI or algorithms. Getting to know someone's taste is part of the fun.

Static on the line

What is your view on AI in general and music in particular?

Well, this could easily become an entire article of its own, haha. I'll try to keep myself under control.

In general, I think AI can be very helpful. I already use it at work, and I have to admit that I really like what it can do there. With music, though, my feelings are almost the complete opposite. I can see a small role for it in suggesting ideas or helping with certain parts of the process. It can also make things accessible that used to cost a lot of money, and that could give more people an opportunity to create music.

But fully AI-generated tracks? As far as I'm concerned, those can go straight in the bin. You can tell me that creating a good prompt requires knowledge of music theory and an understanding of how to use the technology. It still lacks the soul and meaning that make creating music matter to me. It reminds me of big music corporations producing songs purely to make money, only a million times worse.

So yes, there are possibilities worth acknowledging. But full-on AI music? No way, José. As you can probably tell, this brings up quite a few feelings. Let's save the rest for that other article.

Writing changes the listening.
Headphones on

Has running @cube_rat changed the way you listen to music as a private listener?

It has opened my ears to so much more. Before cube_rat, I wasn't discovering anything like this amount of new music from different parts of the world.

I also try to spend time with music I don't immediately understand. Recently, that has meant going deeper into amapiano, gqom and afro house. Moving to Tanzania has probably played a part in that curiosity and in discovering more contemporary African electronic music. Writing changes the listening experience, too. When you try to explain why something works for you, you start paying closer attention to individual tracks and how an entire release fits together. I think it has also made me a little more critical about what I really want to spend my time listening to.

A thousand posts later

After more than a thousand posts, has your taste or your approach to reviewing changed since you started @cube_rat? If so, how?

Looking back, there are whole areas of music I listen to now that barely existed on my radar when I started. Some genres were probably completely unknown to me: beatless hip hop, baroque and chamber pop, noise rock, and the African electronic genres I mentioned, along with afro tech. My taste has grown in directions I couldn't have planned.

My approach to writing has changed as well. In the beginning, I sometimes posted about releases I didn't particularly like. Eventually, I started thinking more about the fact that music is art, and there's a person behind it. Or a music corporation, haha. Either way, publicly putting down someone's work isn't really what I want to do with this account. Of course, it isn't quite that straightforward. There's AI-generated music and music made mainly with dollar signs in mind. But most of that wouldn't find its way onto my feed anyway.

I also try to make a conscious effort to be inclusive. A large share of what I listen to still comes from Europe and the US, but I want to keep discovering artists from other parts of the world. The same goes for making space for women on the account. Women make incredible music and are still underrepresented in the scene. If cube_rat can play even a small part in changing that, I want to do my best.

The crate

What's a record or artist you discovered through running cube_rat that genuinely surprised you or changed the way you think about music?

This is where it gets difficult to give a short answer. There are quite a few!

ULTRAPOP by The Armed is an obvious one. I knew the band already, but this album completely blew my mind. Those huge, catchy melodies crashing into walls of noise, wild hardcore riffs and ridiculously heavy moments—it's such an incredible combination. For me, it's one of the most amazing albums released since the turn of the millennium.

Then there's IRA by Iosonouncane, which I'm 100% sure I would never have come across without cube_rat. It came out in 2021, the same year as ULTRAPOP. What a year for those two records alone. Everything about IRA draws me in. The soundscape can feel like a pressure cooker, with tension building and building, before opening into something as beautiful as a meadow full of flowers. It has given me actual physical sensations that go far beyond getting chills. One of its most distinctive features is the language: words from several languages are combined into something deliberately unfamiliar. Even the words leave you feeling displaced, and that becomes part of the experience. At almost two hours, the whole thing feels like a film. Lie down in the dark, close your eyes and let it take you through it.

Coilguns, the Swiss hardcore band, are another big one for me. Watchwinders and Millennials are so interesting, surprising and unpredictable. Both have this raw sound that makes everything feel even more intense. Their later collaboration EP with Birds in Row also gave us "You & I in the Gap", which I honestly think is one of the best hardcore tracks released in years. Pure genius.

And speaking of Birds in Row, I never really connected with them before Gris Klein in 2022. That album changed things. It's a masterpiece of modern hardcore, and the way "Noah" flows into "Cathedrals" is just unbelievable.

I should probably stop there, but a few more deserve a mention. These are artists I believe I've found, in one way or another, through running cube_rat and have come to love:

What's next for @cube_rat?

I'd love to open my own website, give cube_rat a little more visibility and have somewhere to write longer pieces when I feel like it. Instagram and social media don't really give those texts the space they need.

Let's see what happens. For now, I'm happy as long as musicians keep putting out amazing releases and I get to listen to them and share what I find. Nine years in, there's still so much music waiting around the corner.
